title: On Photography
body:
I don't necessarily see a lot of photography as art. While there are photographers qua "artists" who utilize the medium to portray things, most of the time I think people are using photography to display other people or nature's doing. Where the art is in photography is the individual's selection of their gear, framing, editing, grouping, and exposure. Producing an appealing or "professional"-appearing photo is significantly less difficult than most other forms of what we consider art, though. An amateur musician cannot accidentally stumble upon a masterpiece as easily as a photographer can be granted an opportunity to capture something impressive. There are so many crutches that enable a photographer to feign artistic motive. Specifically, utilizing something like a film camera can enable a user's inexperience to appear as endearing or intentional.

Is there something wrong with this? Not at all. Would I qualify most self-described photographers as artists, though? Also no. A lot of the photos portrayed on this website fall victim to this exact problem I am proposing. They may be visually appealing, and I have learned how to utilize my eye and gear to produce an appealing photo, but those photos are not something I am producing with the intention of communicating a deeper message. After-the-fact meaning may be assigned to them by myself or the viewer, but I think the intention behind the creation of the product is where art often lies. The [NameYourVices project](https://nickckincaid.com/projects/nameyourvices/) is where an artistic vision is preconceived before shots. I use other projects on this website to sharpen my skills with my tool set and produce appealing images. Photography is victim to the fact that, unless doing something like editorial studio photography, you aren't granted the ability to even consider what you want to say before the shutter clicks. If photographers did such, stunning moments would be missed. I am not trying to say there is anything wrong with photography as a medium. I mostly just see it as something less preconceived than its relatives. This also doesn't diminish the form; it is merely different and should be acknowledged.
